# Model Evaluation — FIFA World Cup 2026 Forecast

**Forecast frozen:** 10 June 2026 (before the opening match)
**Evaluated:** 5 August 2026 (after the final)
**Repository:** code, data, tests, and CI included; every figure below is regenerated by `python evaluation/verify.py`
**Model:** Blended Elo/market ratings → calibrated bivariate Poisson goal model → 100,000-run Monte Carlo tournament simulation
**Evaluation sample:** 72 group-stage match forecasts (3-outcome ordinal) + 336 team-stage advancement forecasts (48 teams × 7 stages)

---

## 1. Headline result

| Metric | Model | Benchmark | Skill |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ranked Probability Score** (group matches, n=72) | **0.1618** | 0.2315 (uniform) | **+30.1%** |
| RPS vs. climatology | 0.1618 | 0.2259 | +28.4% |
| Multiclass Brier | 0.5240 | 0.6667 | +21.4% |
| Log loss (ignorance) | 0.8927 | 1.0986 | +18.7% |
| Hit rate (argmax) | 62.5% | 43.1% | +19.4pp |
| **Advancement Brier (aggregate, 7 stages)** | **0.0795** | 0.1297 (base rate) | **+38.7%** |
| Champion log score | 1.588 | 1.808 (betting market) | **beat market by 0.220 nats** |

**Bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples):** RPS ∈ [0.1441, 0.1813]; log loss ∈ [0.8045, 0.9835].
Improvement over uniform: 0.0695 RPS, 95% CI [0.0437, 0.0949], P(improvement > 0) = 1.000.

**Overall grade: B+ / A−.** Strong discrimination and near-unbiased calibration on match outcomes, genuine skill over the betting market on the title question, and two systematic flaws identified below that are correctable and were not known in advance.

---

## 2. Why these metrics

The Ranked Probability Score (Epstein 1969; popularised for football by Constantinou & Fenton 2012) is the field-standard scoring rule for 1X2 match forecasts because it is *sensitive to distance* — the win/draw/loss outcomes are ordinal, so a forecast leaning toward a draw is penalised less by a narrow home win than one leaning toward an away win. Log loss (the ignorance score) is reported alongside because Wheatcroft (2021) argues persuasively that a *local* proper scoring rule is preferable for model selection. Both are proper scoring rules, so neither can be gamed by misreporting beliefs.

For the binary advancement questions (does team X reach stage Y?) the Brier score with a Brier Skill Score against the base rate is standard, decomposed via Murphy (1973) into reliability, resolution, and uncertainty.

---

## 3. Literature context — read this carefully

Published football forecasting models cluster around **RPS ≈ 0.19–0.21** on domestic league matches. Constantinou (2018) reports an average RPS of 0.211 across 52 leagues worldwide and 0.203 for the EPL specifically; a 13-season EPL study using pi-ratings and Bayesian networks reports an overall RPS of 0.195; Hubáček et al. (2018) report approximately 0.20.

**Our 0.1618 is NOT evidence of beating the literature.** World Cup group stages contain far more lopsided fixtures (Germany 7–1 Curaçao, Senegal 5–0 Iraq) than a domestic league where teams are pre-filtered for similar quality. Mismatched fixtures are easy to forecast, which mechanically lowers RPS. The honest statement is: *the model achieved 0.1618 on a fixture set whose difficulty is not comparable to league benchmarks, with a within-sample skill score of +30% over uniform and +28% over the observed climatology.* The skill scores, not the raw RPS, are the transferable claim.

---

## 4. Calibration

All 216 forecast probabilities (72 matches × 3 outcomes), binned:

| Bin | n | Mean forecast | Observed | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.00–0.10 | 5 | 7.4% | 0.0% | −7.4pp |
| 0.10–0.25 | 66 | 20.6% | 9.1% | **−11.5pp** |
| 0.25–0.45 | 89 | 30.0% | 30.3% | +0.3pp |
| 0.45–0.65 | 46 | 52.6% | 67.4% | **+14.8pp** |
| 0.65–1.00 | 10 | 71.0% | 80.0% | +9.0pp |

**Murphy decomposition:** Brier 0.1758 = Reliability 0.0092 − Resolution 0.0557 + Uncertainty 0.2222

Reliability of 0.0092 (where 0 is perfect) is good — the model is close to unbiased on average. Resolution of 0.0557 confirms it genuinely discriminates rather than issuing base-rate forecasts for everything.

But the bin pattern is monotone and one-directional: **the model was systematically under-confident.** Low probabilities should have been lower, high probabilities higher.

---

## 5. Two systematic flaws found

### Flaw 1 — over-shrinkage (under-confidence)

The pre-tournament model compressed all rating gaps by a factor of 0.72, calibrated so that simulated title-probability dispersion matched betting-market dispersion. Post-hoc temperature scaling shows this was too aggressive:

| Temperature | RPS | Log loss |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 0.1475 | 0.8675 |
| 0.7 | 0.1509 | 0.8640 |
| **1.0 (as submitted)** | **0.1618** | **0.8927** |
| 1.3 | 0.1720 | 0.9218 |

Optimal T ≈ 0.53, which would have improved RPS by 8.9%. The *direction* is unambiguous (every sharpening step improved both scoring rules); the *magnitude* is not reliably estimated from n=72 and should not be hard-coded. A defensible correction is a mild sharpening (T ≈ 0.8), not the post-hoc optimum, which is almost certainly overfit to one tournament.

Root cause: the market was used as a calibration target for *dispersion*, but the market prices a favourite-longshot bias into tournament outrights. Anchoring to it imported that bias.

### Flaw 2 — goal-scale and dispersion misspecification

- Predicted 184 total group-stage goals; actual **216** (+17.5% under-prediction). Baseline scoring rate of 1.25 goals/team should have been ≈1.47.
- Goals per team-match: mean 1.500, **variance 2.153** — a variance-to-mean ratio of 1.44. The independent-Poisson assumption requires 1.0.

The data are overdispersed relative to Poisson. A negative binomial or a bivariate Poisson with a correlation term would fit better, and this also partly explains the under-confidence: too little goal variance and too little rating spread pushed probability mass toward draws.

---

## 6. Stage-by-stage advancement performance

| Stage | Brier | Base rate | BSS | Top-N hit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Win group | 0.0943 | 0.1875 | +49.7% | 10/12 |
| Qualify (R32) | 0.1559 | 0.2222 | +29.8% | 26/32 |
| Reach R16 | 0.1305 | 0.2222 | +41.3% | 14/16 |
| Reach QF | 0.0931 | 0.1389 | +32.9% | **4/8** |
| Reach SF | 0.0426 | 0.0764 | +44.3% | 4/4 |
| Reach final | 0.0260 | 0.0399 | +34.8% | 2/2 |
| Champion | 0.0143 | 0.0204 | +29.9% | 1/1 |
| **Aggregate** | **0.0795** | **0.1297** | **+38.7%** | — |

The quarterfinal round is the visible weak point (4/8). Four teams reached the QF from ≤26% pre-tournament probability (Switzerland 19%, Morocco 21%, Norway 25%, Belgium 26%), while two group winners we rated above 90% to qualify — Germany and the Netherlands — exited the Round of 32 on penalties. Penalty shootouts were modelled as near-coinflips, which is defensible, but it means the Round of 32 was the highest-variance round in the tournament and the model had no mechanism to anticipate that.

Notably, the pre-tournament sensitivity analysis (Scenario E, "elevated knockout upset rates") identified exactly this failure mode and projected the champion probability falling from 20.4% to 14.7%. The failure mode was correctly identified and still under-weighted in the base case.

---

## 7. Limitations — the section that matters most

1. **n = 1 tournament.** This is the binding constraint on every claim here. A single World Cup cannot establish forecasting skill. The champion was correctly identified, but a 20.4% forecast being realised is weak evidence either way — it is exactly what a well-calibrated model looks like 20% of the time and what a lucky model looks like some of the time too.
2. **No out-of-sample backtest.** Ratings were hand-assembled for one event. There is no held-out validation, no walk-forward evaluation, and no demonstration that the pipeline generalises. This is the single largest gap between this project and a publishable result.
3. **Market contamination.** Roughly 35% of each rating came from betting odds. The model is therefore *not independent* of the market, and "beating the market" on the champion log score partly reflects a 4-point deviation on one team that happened to be right. With one observation this is not a claim of market inefficiency.
4. **Post-hoc metric selection risk.** The metrics here were chosen after seeing results. They are the field-standard ones, but the temperature optimum in particular is fit on the evaluation data and is reported as a diagnostic, not a validated correction.
5. **Third-place bracket allocation** used a constrained greedy approximation of FIFA's 495-scenario Annex C, not the exact table.
6. **Selection bias in narrative claims.** The pre-tournament report made roughly ten dark-horse and over/under-rated calls. Several hit (Argentina underrated → reached the final; Norway → QF; Colombia → won Group K). Several missed badly (Türkiye projected as a QF surprise → finished last in their group). Reporting only the hits would be dishonest; the aggregate Brier scores are the only unbiased summary.

---

## 8. What version 2 would change

| Change | Rationale |
|---|---|
| Backtest on WC 2010/2014/2018/2022 + Euros with walk-forward validation | Only way to make any skill claim credible |
| Replace independent Poisson with bivariate Poisson or negative binomial | Observed variance/mean = 1.44 |
| Raise baseline scoring rate ~1.25 → ~1.45 | 17.5% goal under-prediction |
| Reduce shrinkage (T ≈ 0.8, tuned on backtest, not on 2026) | Systematic under-confidence across all bins |
| Fit market blend weight on historical data rather than assuming 35% | Removes an arbitrary hyperparameter |
| Implement exact Annex C third-place table | Removes an approximation |
| Freeze each forecast with `scripts/prereg.py` **before** kickoff | Makes falsifiability verifiable by third parties rather than author-attested |
| Publish per-matchweek forecasts on a live competition | Grows n from 1 toward a sample that can actually support a skill claim |

---

## 9. Reproducibility and pre-registration

The pre-tournament forecast was generated on 10 June 2026, before the opening match, and this evaluation consumes only that frozen output. Nothing in the model was refit after results were known — the temperature analysis in §5 is a diagnostic and is explicitly *not* applied to any headline number.

Reproduce end to end:

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
python forecast/model.py --sims 100000     # seed-reproducible
python evaluation/verify.py                # every number in this document
python -m pytest tests/ -q                 # 19 tests
```

The rewritten `forecast/model.py` reproduces the frozen forecast to Monte Carlo precision (Spain 20.4%, Argentina 12.3%, France 12.1%, England 8.8%).

**Pre-registration, stated honestly.** `scripts/prereg.py` hashes the frozen inputs and outputs into a manifest; committing it creates a timestamped, tamper-evident record, and CI re-verifies the hashes on every push. But the WC2026 manifest was created *after* the tournament — the tool itself reports `frozen before: False` against the 11 June kickoff deadline. The forecast content predates the tournament; the cryptographic chain of custody does not. For this event you are trusting the author, not the hashes. The tooling exists so that subsequent forecasts do not require that trust, and no stronger claim should be read into it.

**Test coverage** targets the properties that matter rather than line coverage: that RPS, Brier, and log loss are *proper* (honest reporting minimises expected score, verified against 40,000 sampled outcomes), that RPS is distance-sensitive, that the Murphy decomposition reconstructs the Brier score, that advancement probabilities are monotone across stages, and that champion probabilities sum to 1.

One genuine bug was found by these tests after the forecast was frozen: outcome probabilities summed to 0.99984 rather than 1.0 for the most lopsided fixtures, because the scoreline grid truncated at 10 goals. The grid now extends to 16 and outcome probabilities are renormalised. The effect on every reported metric was below the fourth decimal place; the fix is recorded in the commit history rather than silently applied.
